   • Casting a deciding vote in the event of a tie (in many organizations)  
   • Representing the board or committee in external dealings  

2. Usage and Variations  
   • “Chairman” is the traditional, male-neutral title.  
   • Many organizations now use “chair,” “chairperson” or simply “chair” for gender neutrality.

3. Qualifications and Selection  
   • Often elected by the full board or membership at an annual meeting  
   • May require prior board service or specific expertise  
   • Sometimes appointed by a higher authority (e.g. a nominating committee)  

4. Why It Matters  
   • A strong, impartial chair helps ensure fair discussion and decision-making.  
   • Good chairs balance control (keeping order) with openness (encouraging input).

In simpler terms, it asks: Who gets sick? When? Where? Why? And how can we prevent or control it?

Key concepts and components  
•  Distribution  
  – Descriptive epidemiology: characterizes health events by person (age, sex, behavior), place (geography, environment) and time (seasonality, trends).  
•  Determinants  
  – Analytic epidemiology: investigates causal (or risk) factors through study designs such as cohort studies, case–control studies and randomized trials.  
•  Measures  
  – Incidence: new cases per population over a period of time.  
  – Prevalence: total existing cases at a point (or period) in time.  
  – Risk, rates and ratios (e.g., attack rate, mortality rate, relative risk, odds ratio).  
•  Populations  
  – Focus is on groups rather than individuals, though clinical epidemiology bridges to patient-level questions.  

Core functions in public health  
 1. Surveillance: continuous, systematic collection and analysis of health data to monitor disease patterns and detect outbreaks.  
 2. Outbreak investigation: field studies to identify sources and modes of transmission, followed by control measures.  
 3. Analytical studies: testing hypotheses about exposures and outcomes to identify risk or protective factors.  
 4. Evaluation of interventions: measuring effectiveness and safety of vaccines, screening programs or public-health policies.  
 5. Policy and prevention: translating findings into guidelines, recommendations and health-promotion strategies.  

Branches and specializations  
•  Infectious-disease epidemiology (e.g., influenza, COVID-19)  
•  Chronic-disease epidemiology (e.g., cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular disease)  
•  Genetic and molecular epidemiology  
•  Environmental and occupational epidemiology  
•  Social and behavioral epidemiology  

A brief historical note  
  – Hippocrates (5th century BCE) first suggested environment and lifestyle influence health.  
  – John Snow’s mid-19th-century cholera investigations in London laid the groundwork for modern field epidemiology and the use of maps to track disease clusters.  

In sum, epidemiology is the cornerstone of public health and preventive medicine.
